query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment that promotes selective oxidation of Cu in the FeNiCrCoCu thin coating will form a continuous, lubricious Cu-rich oxide layer that reduces overall wear and alters the microscopic deformation mechanism during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating with a homogeneous fine-grained microstructure and uniformly distributed elements on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a pre-oxidation annealing step at approximately 600 °C in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment for a short, defined duration to selectively oxidize Cu.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests conducted at 600–800 °C under ambient atmospheric conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, thin Cu-rich oxide layer at the surface of the coating.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the more oxidation‐sensitive Cu promotes phase segregation at the surface, creating a protective oxide film that acts as a lubricant and barrier. This layer is expected to modify the microscopic deformation behavior (e.g., by reducing dislocation activity or grain-boundary sliding aggressiveness) and lower the overall wear rate during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as-deposited coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit reduced wear (lower weight loss and coefficient of friction) and a shift in microscopic deformation modes, observable as differences in surface microstructure (e.g., less severe plastic deformation or altered grain-boundary features).
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: The predicted effects are expected to hold under high-temperature sliding in the range of 600–800 °C; behavior outside this temperature range or under different oxygen partial pressures may not follow the same mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the wear reduction and the detailed changes in microscopic deformation are uncertain and may depend on the precise kinetics of Cu oxidation and oxide layer stability during sliding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu-coated samples: one set receives the pre-oxidation annealing treatment (600 °C in a controlled oxygen environment for a defined duration), while the other set remains as-deposited. Subject both sets to identical reciprocating sliding tests at 600–800 °C. Characterize wear rates, friction coefficients, and microscopic deformation features (via SEM, TEM, or in situ high-temperature XRD) post-test.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Surface oxide layer composition and continuity
Microstructural analysis of deformation features (grain boundaries, dislocation structures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and a corresponding modification in deformation mechanisms compared to the as-deposited baseline, or if no continuous Cu-rich oxide layer is observed on the pre-oxidized samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Earlier work on high-entropy alloy coatings has evolved from understanding bulk creep and deformation at intermediate temperatures to investigating wear behavior under high-temperature sliding. In studies such as PMC7515071, researchers observed that at elevated temperatures (800–900 °C) the formation of oxide phases (e.g., spinels) correlated with improved wear resistance, although the precise mechanism was not isolated. Simultaneously, debates have continued regarding whether mechanisms such as dynamic recrystallization, grain-boundary sliding, or oxidation‐induced phase segregation (involving elements like Cu) primarily govern the wear and microscopic deformation.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear which single interfacial or microstructural process predominantly controls macroscopic wear resistance and the microscopic deformation mode in thin FeNiCrCoCu coatings during high-temperature sliding. In particular, the role of selective oxidation (and consequent phase segregation of Cu) versus grain-boundary processes has not been decisively tested.
decision.lever: Introduce a pre-oxidation annealing step—in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment at around 600 °C for a defined short duration—to selectively promote Cu oxidation relative to the as-deposited homogeneous coating.
decision.why: The trend in prior studies indicates that high-temperature sliding wear resistance improves when a protective oxide (or spinel-type) layer forms at the surface. Given that Cu is the most oxidation‐sensitive element in the FeNiCrCoCu system, a controlled pre-oxidation treatment is expected to drive its segregation into an oxide phase. This should yield a lubricious, protective layer that reduces wear and alters deformation mechanisms. The proposed experiment directly tests whether selective oxidation of Cu governs the wear and deformation behavior under the high-temperature sliding regime (600–800 °C). A failure to observe the predicted reduction in wear and microstructural changes (or the emergence of an expected oxide phase) would falsify the hypothesis.
